bib.title: Clipper: A Low-Latency Online Prediction Serving System
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv:1612.03079v2 [cs.DC], 28 Feb 2017; the PDF prints no venue)

question: How can a general-purpose serving layer give low-latency, high-throughput and more accurate online predictions across heterogeneous ML frameworks without modifying them?
hypothesis: A layered design (model abstraction layer with caching and adaptive batching, plus a bandit-based model selection layer) can match a framework-integrated server's throughput and latency while adding model composition and online learning.
contributions: A layered architecture that abstracts away the complexity associated with serving predictions in existing machine learning frameworks (Sec 3).
A set of novel techniques to reduce and bound latency while maximizing throughput that generalize across machine learning frameworks (Sec 4).
A model selection layer that enables online model selection and composition to provide robust and accurate predictions for interactive applications (Sec 5).

method.summary: Clipper, written in Rust, sits between applications (REST/RPC) and models in Docker containers. A model abstraction layer adds a per-model prediction cache (CLOCK eviction), per-container adaptive batching (AIMD against a latency SLO) and replicated containers; a model selection layer uses Exp3 (single model) or Exp4 (linear ensemble) bandit policies with straggler mitigation and per-user state in Redis. Evaluated by microbenchmarks on MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet and TIMIT, and against TensorFlow Serving.
method.task: online prediction serving (object recognition, speech recognition)

datasets.name: TIMIT speech
datasets.size: 6300 recordings, 5 sec., 39 labels; 630 speakers in eight dialects
datasets.split: users randomly drawn from the test corpus, interaction simulated from pre-recorded speech

models.name: Clipper
models.architecture: two-layer serving system, Rust, per-model Docker containers with RPC

other.frameworks_supported: Spark MLLib, Scikit-Learn, Caffe, TensorFlow, HTK (each under 25 lines of code)

models.name: TensorFlow Serving
models.architecture: model and serving in same process, static batch sizes with timeout

models.name: Scikit-Learn / PySpark MNIST models (linear SVM, kernel SVM, random forest, logistic regression, Spark linear SVM, no-op)
Caffe VGG, GoogLeNet, ResNet, CaffeNet; TensorFlow Inception (ensemble members)
models.layers: VGG 13 Conv and 3 FC; GoogLeNet 96 Conv and 5 FC; ResNet 151 Conv and 1 FC; CaffeNet 5 Conv and 3 FC; Inception 6 Conv, 1 FC, 3 Incept.

parameters.aimd_backoff: batch size reduced by 10% when batch latency exceeds the SLO; additive increase step not stated
parameters.delayed_batching: 2ms batch delay in Fig 5 example; timeout swept to 4000 us
parameters.exp3: weight s_i = 1 per model, p_i = s_i/sum s_j, update s_i <- s_i exp(-eta L(y, yhat)/p_i), loss in [0,1]; eta value not stated
parameters.exp4_ensemble: linear weighted average of base predictions, confidence = number of models agreeing; missing predictions replaced by their average value at the latency deadline
parameters.tf_serving_batch_sizes: MNIST 512, CIFAR 128, ImageNet 16 (hand-tuned for TensorFlow Serving)
parameters.failure_simulation: five Caffe CIFAR models, 20K sequential queries, best model degraded after 5K queries and recovered after 10K

other.hardware: all machines 2 Intel Haswell-EP CPUs, 256 GB RAM, Ubuntu 14.04, Linux 4.2.0; TensorFlow on Nvidia Tesla K20c, 5 GB GPU memory, 2496 cores; scaling cluster on 10Gbps and 1Gbps switch; single server unless noted

metrics.name: throughput
metrics.definition: queries per second; peak/maximum sustained for TF Serving comparison

metrics.name: latency (mean, P99)
metrics.definition: time to render a prediction given a query

metrics.name: error rate
metrics.definition: Top-1 (CIFAR-10), Top-5 (ImageNet), cumulative average error, speech error

eval.protocol: microbenchmarks per feature; number of runs, seeds and confidence intervals not stated; Fig 11 shows p99 as error bars

results.claim: Batching raises throughput up to 26x for the Scikit-Learn SVM while meeting a 20ms SLO.
results.setup: MNIST models in Scikit-Learn/Spark, adaptive batching vs no batching, 20ms latency SLO, Fig 4
results.quote: can improve throughput by up to 26x
results.note: Text says 'Scikit-Learn SVM'; Sec 4.3.1 says 'Scikit-Learn linear SVM'.

results.claim: Max batch size within a 20ms SLO differs 241x between the linear SVM and the kernel SVM.
results.setup: Scikit-Learn linear vs kernel SVM on MNIST, 20ms SLO, Fig 3

results.claim: Under that SLO the linear SVM reaches nearly 30,000 qps while the kernel SVM is limited to 200 qps.
results.quote: the kernel SVM is limited to 200 qps under this SLO

results.claim: AIMD backs off the batch size by 10% on SLO violation and performs nearly identically to quantile regression but is simpler.
results.setup: Spark and Scikit-Learn models, Fig 4; AIMD default

results.claim: A 2ms batch delay gives a 3.3x throughput gain for the Scikit-Learn SVM but none for the Spark SVM.
results.quote: a 2ms batch delay provides a 3.3x improvement

results.claim: Replicating GPU containers across four nodes on 10Gbps scales throughput 3.95x (19,500 to 77,000 qps); 1Gbps saturates at the second remote machine.
results.quote: Clipper gets a 3.95x throughput increase from 19,500 qps

results.claim: Prediction caching raises feedback processing throughput 1.6x, from about 6K to 11K observations per second.
results.setup: four-model ensemble (random forest, logistic regression, linear SVM in Scikit-Learn, linear SVM in Spark)
results.quote: prediction caching increased feedback processing throughput in Clipper by 1.6x

results.claim: Linear ensembles of five off-the-shelf CNNs cut ImageNet error by 5.2% relative.
results.setup: ImageNet, five models from Table 2, Fig 7 (Top-5 about 0.0618 single vs 0.0586 ensemble read from figure)
results.quote: achieves a 5.2% relative reduction in the error rate
results.note: Figure 7 bar labels are ambiguous in extracted text.

results.claim: Python TensorFlow containers lose 15-18% throughput vs TensorFlow Serving; C++ containers are nearly identical.
results.setup: MNIST CNN, CIFAR-10 AlexNet, ImageNet Inception-v3, GPU, hand-tuned batch sizes, Fig 11
results.quote: The Python model containers suffer a 15-18% performance hit
results.note: Fig 11 labels (legend order TF Serving, Clipper TF-C++, Clipper TF-Python): MNIST 23138/22269/19537, CIFAR 5519/5472/4571, ImageNet 56/52/47; mapping to systems inferred from legend order.

results.claim: Clipper TensorFlow Serving comparison, MNIST throughput: 23138 (TF Serving) vs 19537 (Clipper TF-Python).
Clipper renders low and bounded latency predictions under 20ms in the authors' evaluation.
Each of five frameworks was added with fewer than 25 lines of code.
results.setup: Spark MLLib, Scikit-Learn, Caffe, TensorFlow, HTK
results.quote: each was added using fewer than 25 lines of code

limits: Models are black boxes: Clipper does not optimize execution within frameworks, so slow models remain slow.
Clipper does not manage training or retraining; if all models are stale it cannot beat what ensembles give.
The network becomes the bottleneck for large inputs on 1Gbps links.
No seeds, run counts or variance reported; cache size and Exp3 eta not stated; Fig 11 compares only three TensorFlow models with batch sizes hand-tuned for TensorFlow Serving.
2016-17 hardware (K20c) and models; no LLM or token-level workloads.

terms.definition: the expected time to evaluate a batch of a given size
the batch size that maximizes throughput subject to the constraint that the batch evaluation latency is under the target SLO
